summary: Updates RFC 4871 on DKIM signatures, clarifying the nature, roles and relationship of two identifier tag values that may be handed to a receiving processing module. It was replaced by RFC 6376.

eli5.summary: Mail signatures carry two name tags. This clears up what each one means and which to use. It was later replaced by RFC 6376.

questions: what is dkim identifier tag d= i=
subtitle: Clarify what DKIM signatures tell you about who sent an email.

tldr.problem: RFC 4871 on DKIM signatures carries two identifier values (d= and i=) in a signature, but leaves it unclear which one is the primary output that mail readers should trust, creating interoperability problems and confusion about what DKIM actually guarantees.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC clarifies that d= (Signing Domain Identifier or SDID) is the mandatory output to assessors that DKIM provides, while i= (Agent or User Identifier or AUID) is optional metadata that may be passed but is not DKIM's primary responsibility.
tldr.outcome: Mail systems implementing DKIM now have a clear interface: they output a single domain that claims responsibility, allowing mail filters and assessors to make consistent trust decisions. RFC 6376 later superseded this specification.

today: RFC 5672 updates RFC 4871 and clarifies the semantics of DKIM signature identifiers for mail receivers and processors. It establishes the d= tag as the primary output for trust assessment. RFC 6376 later superseded both RFC 4871 and RFC 5672 with a consolidated specification of DKIM.

sections.title: The Confusion in RFC 4871
sections.content:
DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) allows a signing domain to assert responsibility for a message by adding a digital signature to the email header. The ultimate goal is to communicate an identifier to a mail assessor—a module that evaluates whether to trust the message based on the signing domain.

However, RFC 4871 defines two identifier values in the DKIM-Signature header: d= (domain of the signer) and i= (identity of the user or agent on behalf of whom the message is signed). The RFC never clearly states which identifier should be delivered to the assessor or what the relationship between them is. This ambiguity means signers and assessors may interpret the two values differently, causing interoperability problems.

A signer might intend i= to be assessed, but the verifier might deliver d= to the assessor instead, leading to wrong trust decisions. This RFC resolves that confusion by defining clear roles for each identifier and specifying a standardized interface.
sections.eli5: A mail signature used to carry two names, and nobody was sure which name the assessor should check. This caused confusion and wrong decisions.

sections.title: Identifiers: SDID, AUID, and Identity
sections.content:
This RFC introduces three new semantic concepts. Identity is a person, role, or organization (the author, author's organization, an ISP, or a mailing list operator). Identifier is a label that refers to an identity (a domain name). Signing Domain Identifier (SDID) is the single mandatory payload output of DKIM—a domain name that claims responsibility for introducing a message into the mail stream. Agent or User Identifier (AUID) is an optional identifier in the format of an email address (local-part@domain) that refers to the agent or user on behalf of whom the SDID is taking responsibility.

The SDID is specified in the d= tag of the DKIM-Signature header. The AUID is specified in the i= tag. For DKIM processing, these identifiers have basic domain name semantics; any owner-specific semantics are outside the scope of DKIM and are handled by higher-layer applications.
sections.eli5: A domain name is the identity claiming responsibility (like 'example.com'). An email address is the person or service on behalf of whom that domain claims responsibility (like 'admin@example.com'). The domain is mandatory; the email is optional extra information.

sections.title: The d= and i= Tags in DKIM-Signature
sections.content:
The d= tag specifies the SDID, the domain claiming responsibility for message introduction. This domain MUST correspond to a valid DNS name under which the DKIM public key record is published. Verifiers MUST use the SDID to query for the public key. The conventions and semantics used by a signer to create a specific SDID are outside the scope of DKIM; any interpretation of those semantics by an assessor is at the assessor's discretion.

The i= tag specifies the AUID, the identifier on behalf of which the SDID is taking responsibility. The syntax is a standard email address where the local-part MAY be omitted. The domain portion MUST be the same as or a subdomain of the d= value. The AUID is specified as having email address syntax, but it is NOT required to resolve in DNS or have mailbox semantics. The signer determines the namespace; verifiers and assessors should not assume they know what it means beyond the scope of DKIM.
sections.eli5: The d= tag is the door label. The i= tag is the person's name on a note left at that door. You must trust the door to know the message is real, but the name on the note can be anything the door's owner wants.

sections.title: DKIM's Mandatory Output and Verification
sections.content:
The mandatory output of DKIM verification to a receiving Identity Assessor is two pieces of information: a yes/no result indicating whether the signature verified, and the single Signing Domain Identifier (the d= value). This output is sufficient for an assessor to make trust decisions or apply reputation judgments based on the SDID.

Additional information, such as the AUID (i= value), MAY be provided to the assessor or to other processing modules at the discretion of the DKIM implementation. However, claiming DKIM compliance requires at minimum delivering the verification result and the SDID to a consuming module. DKIM implementation developers may provide additional context to higher-level services, but that additional context is outside the scope of DKIM's specification.

When a verifier detects a signature that does not meet requirements (for example, if the d= domain is not the same as or a parent of the i= domain), it MUST consider the signature invalid. The relationship between SDID and AUID is specified: the i= domain must be the same as or a subdomain of the d= domain, potentially limited further by the 's' flag in the key record.
sections.eli5: DKIM promises to deliver exactly two things: 'Is this real?' and 'What domain claims responsibility?' Everything else is optional bonus information for mail filters.

sections.title: Security and Interoperability Implications
sections.content:
This clarification of DKIM's payload affects security, interoperability, and the correct interpretation of DKIM's semantics. The RFC cautions that while it is tempting to link the SDID or AUID to the From: header field (the visible sender shown to the user), this linkage is a heuristic policy issue outside the scope of DKIM. Trust is complex and subject to attack; the RFC recommends strict limitations on reliance on such linkages.

By clearly defining what DKIM outputs and what downstream modules must do with that output, this RFC reduces the likelihood of misinterpretation and subtle security mistakes. Signers now have clear guidance: publish a responsible SDID and decide whether to use i= for finer-grained accountability. Assessors have a single, stable identifier to build their trust judgments on. The clarification improves both security and interoperability by establishing a single, standardized API between DKIM and the modules that consume its results.
sections.eli5: Mail filters now know for certain what they can trust, instead of guessing. This makes the system more secure and less likely to cause embarrassing mistakes.

viz.caption: DKIM output: mandatory vs. optional information

items.title: Mandatory Output
items.text: Verification result (yes/no) and the Signing Domain Identifier (d= value)

items.title: Optional Information
items.text: Agent or User Identifier (i= value) and other header details, at assessor discretion
